newsitem.title: EGYPT: Demand, price caps drive Egypt bourse to records.
newsitem.headline: Demand, price caps drive Egypt bourse to records.

text.p: Heavy capital inflows squeezed by limits on the rise of stock prices sent Egypt's bourse into record territory but analysts say the market will soon calm down as its valuation reaches the levels of regional rivals.

Egypt's Capital Market Authority (CMA) overall index closed at a record 387.92 points on Monday, its 12th highest level in as many days and almost 29 percent higher than the beginning of the year. The index rose 39.3 percent in the whole of 1996.
"This was expected to happen sooner of later," Neveen El-Tahry of brokerage firm Delta-EAB told Reuters.
"Every man on the street knows there's money to be made in the bourse and the foreign investors are also pouring money in. There are tremendous cash inflows at the moment," she added.
According to the head of the CMA, trading in January amounted to a hefty 1.7 billion pounds ($500 million) compared to just 440 million pounds in the same month a year ago.
Brokers say the investment-grade foreign and local currency credit ratings that the international agency Standard & Poors gave to Egypt last month increased investor appetite for its securities.
They say the ratings will also beef up Egypt's weighting when it is listed on the International Financial Corporation composite investable index IFCINDEX and so attract more funds.

But while analysts admit that genuine demand is pushing the market higher, they say that the trend would not have been so sharp if the CMA did not have a constraining five percent ceiling and floor on the price movement of stocks.
"The five percent ceiling cap is inflating the market," said Amr Abul Magd, managing director of brokers Megavest.
He said investors were holding onto their shares because they expected the stock prices, pressured by the constraints, to rise again in the next session.
"They (CMA) are distorting trading and in a way they are manipulating and pressuring it," said Mohammed Maher, managing director of analysts Prime Investments.
"If they allow the investors to satisfy their demands at any prices, the market will peak and then fall naturally.

"I mean what if a company discovered a cure for cancer? Stock prices would double on such news and there would be a lot of demand. It would last for a few days then settle but with the price cap, the rise would be drawn out," he added.

But even with the price cap extending the rise, analysts say the market will soon steady when average 13 to 14 price-to-earning ratios increase to the average ratio of 16 for a market like Turkey and the higher 18 to 19 levels of more mature emerging markets.

"We're on the last peak and very close to markets like Morocco and Turkey. Investors will soon begin to realise their profits because why should they only invest in Egypt then when they have several other options?" Maher said.

Egypt has made considerable effort to sell itself to the world. It hosted the third Middle East and North Africa Economic Conference in November and President Hosni Mubarak has trumpeted his country's investment potential during foreign trips and most recently at the World Economic Forum at Davos.
But brokers say the state must keep up its privatisation programme -- the flagship of its economic reforms -- for the market to maintain its momentum.

Egyptian officials said the state sold a majority in 16 firms in 1996 and between 10 and 40 percent in nine others. It has set a privatisation target of 52 firms for this year, twelve through the bourse and the rest to anchor investors.
"We're attractive but for how long?" said Tahry. "We're still quite a cheap market but as we rise we will have to compete harder to attract investors and speed up the privatisation programme."
($1 = 3.4 Egyptian pounds)
